docs.text:
Tier Cost What it is 0: Desk Starter $200 to $400 Wheel clamped to your desk 1: Foldable / Apartment $500 to $700 Entry direct drive on a seat that folds into a closet 2: First Dedicated Rig $1,200 to $1,600 Fixed cockpit, 8 to 9 Nm, load cell brake 3: Sweet Spot Enthusiast $1,800 to $2,200 Aluminum rig, 12 Nm, pedals you keep for 10 years 4: Triples / VR Enthusiast $3,500 to $5,500 Tier 3 plus wraparound screens or VR, shifter, shakers 5: Motion / Pro $10,000 to $18,000 The rig moves. What F1 Arcade has
  • Costs exclude PC or console, and the screen until Tier 4

docs.title: F1 Arcade vs home
docs.text:
• F1 Arcade: Vesaro rigs on D-BOX motion, custom rFactor 2, heavy driving assists
  • ~$20 to $45 per person per visit, before food and drink
  • Home: no motion until Tier 5
  • Home: assists off, so harder at first. Normal
  • Home wheel and pedals at Tier 3 are better than the venue's
  • Home: any car, any track, ranked races against real people

docs.title: Three decisions, in order
docs.text:
• Platform: PC, PlayStation or Xbox. It limits which wheels work before budget does
  • Space: desk only, fold away, or permanent
  • Budget: pick the tier

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Spend order: solid mount, then load cell brake, then wheel strength, then screens
  • 5 to 8 Nm of wheel force is plenty to start. 8 to 12 Nm is enough forever for most
  • Direct drive now starts at ~$260. Skip gear-driven wheels unless used
  • Used Logitech G29 at ~$120 resells for ~$120: a free trial
  • PlayStation is the expensive platform at every tier
  • Motion and big torque add immersion, not lap time

docs.title: The six tiers
docs.text: Tier Cost Mount Wheel Brake Screen 0: Desk Starter $200 to $400 Desk clamp 2 to 5.5 Nm Spring Yours 1: Foldable / Apartment $500 to $700 Folding seat or stand 4 to 5.5 Nm direct drive Spring Yours 2: First Dedicated Rig $1,200 to $1,600 Steel cockpit 8 to 9 Nm Entry load cell Yours 3: Sweet Spot Enthusiast $1,800 to $2,200 Aluminum profile 12 Nm Good load cell Yours 4: Triples / VR Enthusiast $3,500 to $5,500 Aluminum profile 12 to 21 Nm Good load cell Triples or VR 5: Motion / Pro $10,000 to $18,000 Profile on motion actuators 25 Nm Active Triples

docs.title: Basic constraints
docs.text:
• Platform
    • PC: everything works, every game
    • Xbox: Moza R3, Fanatec with an Xbox wheel, Logitech, Thrustmaster
    • PlayStation: only Logitech, Thrustmaster, Fanatec GT DD Pro and ClubSport DD+. Costs more at every tier
    • Console: one screen only, no triples, no iRacing
  • Space
    • Desk only: Tier 0
    • Must fold away: Tier 1. Folded ~104×93×30 cm
    • Permanent: ~2.0×1.0 m for a rig and single screen
    • Triples: ~1.8 to 2.1 m wide
  • Neighbors and housemates
    • Gear wheels rattle. Direct drive is quiet
    • Bass shakers and motion travel through floors
  • PC power
    • Single 1440p screen: ~$1,150 PC
    • Ultrawide, entry triples, Quest VR: ~$1,850 to $2,200 PC
    • Triple 1440p, high-res VR: ~$3,200 PC
  • Time
    • Tier 0 and 1 need setup every session. Friction kills the habit
    • A permanent rig gets used more

docs.title: What each jump buys
docs.text:
• 0 to 1: pedals and seat stop moving
  • 1 to 2: nothing flexes, brake by pressure. Consistency
  • 2 to 3: a rig and pedals you never replace
  • 3 to 4: you can see beside you. Immersion
  • 4 to 5: the seat moves. Feel, not speed

docs.title: $200–$400
docs.text: Assumes: existing PC/console, display, desk

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Curious after F1 Arcade, want to try a wheel at home for minimum money
  • Shared room, no dedicated space
  • Not sure it will stick
  • Skip if: desk is wobbly or glass
  • Skip if: already sure you want a rig (go to Tier 2)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R5 bundle ~$380. 5.5 Nm direct drive, wheel, 2 pedals, desk clamp
  • PC, cheaper: Moza R3 bundle ~$260 to $280. 3.9 Nm direct drive
  • Xbox: Moza R3 Xbox bundle ~$320 to $340
  • PlayStation: Thrustmaster T248R $300 (belt/gear hybrid, 3 pedals)
  • PlayStation or Xbox, cheapest: Logitech G29 / G920 ~$200 street. $300 list, never pay list
  • No PlayStation direct drive at this price
  • Not in the box: shifter (Logitech $60). Not needed to start

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• Existing desk ~120×60 cm, wheel clamps to edge
  • Needs ~30 cm desk depth (est)
  • Pedals on floor against wall or box
  • Stores in a box ~45×35×30 cm (est)
  • Setup 10 to 15 min each time

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs F1 Arcade: no motion, no fixed seat, assists off, so harder
  • Logitech G29: notchy, loud gear rattle
  • Moza R3/R5: smooth, quiet, light
  • Slower than a controller for the first week or two
  • Unlimited seat time

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: cheapest way in, nothing to build or store
  • +: resells easily
  • +: Moza parts bolt onto any rig later
  • −: office chair rolls back under braking
  • −: pedals slide on hard floor
  • −: brake is a spring, not a load cell
  • −: clamp on, clamp off every session kills the habit

docs.title: Free fixes
docs.text:
• Chair: caster cups, or rear wheels in old shoes
  • Pedals: against the wall, or screwed to a board the chair sits on
  • Desk shake: push desk to wall, lower force feedback

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Wheel stand or foldable seat so pedals stop moving (Tier 1)
  • Moza brake kit $39: stiffer brake, cheap
  • Carries over: Moza base, wheel, pedals
  • Does not carry over: Logitech and T248 sets are closed systems, sold whole

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• G29/G920 ~$100 to $150 local
  • Resells for what you paid: a free trial
  • Check: centers on power-up, no grinding, all pedals reach full range, power brick included
  • Avoid: G27 and older (no PS5/Xbox), anything without force feedback

docs.title: $500–$700
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC/console, display, foldable space

  • PlayStation with direct drive: $800 to $1,000

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Hooked after Tier 0, or sure you'll stick with it
  • Apartment / shared room, rig must disappear
  • Console on a couch TV
  • Skip if: a permanent 60×140 cm floor spot exists (Tier 2 costs little more)
  • Skip if: you want a stiff load cell brake (foldables flex)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R5 bundle ~$380 + NLR GTLite Pro $299 = ~$680
  • PC, budget: R5 bundle + NLR GTLite $199 = ~$580
  • PC, own chair: R5 bundle + NLR Wheel Stand Lite 2.0 $179 = ~$560
  • Xbox: Moza R3 Xbox bundle ~$340 + Playseat Challenge X $300 = ~$640
  • PlayStation, direct drive: Thrustmaster T598 $600 (5 Nm, wheel, pedals) + GTLite Pro $299 = ~$900
  • PlayStation, in budget: Thrustmaster T248R $300 + GTLite $199 = ~$500. Not direct drive
  • Newest and cheapest foldable: NLR GTLite Air $179 (Sept 2026)

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• GTLite Pro in use: 176×93×95 cm, 14.4 kg
  • Folded: 104×93×30 cm. Closet, not under the bed
  • Challenge X: 11.6 kg
  • First assembly 30 to 60 min (est)
  • Fold or unfold with gear attached: 1 to 2 min (est)

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 0: fixed seat-to-pedal distance, reclined posture, pedals stay put
  • 5 Nm direct drive: smooth and detailed, still light
  • vs F1 Arcade: similar posture, far less rigid, no motion, weaker wheel

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: packs into a closet
  • +: real driving position
  • +: works in front of a couch TV
  • +: base, wheel, pedals all move to a rigid rig later
  • −: flex under hard braking and above ~8 Nm (makers claim 10 to 13 Nm)
  • −: fabric seat sags over time
  • −: shifter mounts wobble
  • −: cables to manage every session
  • −: center post between the legs on some designs
  • −: the foldable itself has no upgrade path

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Rigid rig first, load cell brake second
  • While still on a foldable: a rim you like beats stiffer pedals
  • Resale on the foldable ~half (est)

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Playseat Challenge, NLR GTLite, F-GT Lite: common on Marketplace, ~$100 to $180 (est)
  • Check: seams and velcro, hinges lock under load, wheel plate holes match your base, no bent tubes
  • Avoid: no-name stands made for G29 only (thin plates crack with direct drive)

docs.title: $1,200–$1,600
docs.text: Assumes: existing PC/console, display, dedicated space

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Permanent spot available
  • Drives weekly
  • Wants braking that is the same every lap
  • Skip if: you can stretch ~$400 (Tier 3 profile rig is the buy-once choice)
  • Skip if: it must pack away (Tier 1)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R9 V3 base $329 (9 Nm) + KS wheel $229 + SRP2 pedals $149 (entry load cell) + NLR GTRacer 2.0 cockpit $499 = ~$1,200
  • PC, better pedals: swap in Moza CRP2 $369 = ~$1,430
  • PC, alt: Simagic Alpha Evo Sport 9 Nm bundle (base, wheel, pedals) ~$600 to $790 + cockpit
  • PlayStation: Fanatec GT DD Pro 8 Nm bundle $860 + load cell kit ~$100 to $140 + Fanatec CSL Cockpit with seat $400 = ~$1,400
  • Xbox: Thrustmaster T598 Xbox $600 + GTRacer 2.0 $499 = ~$1,100, before a load cell
  • Xbox, alt: Fanatec CSL Cockpit bundle $1,045 (cockpit, seat, CSL DD 5 Nm, wheel, pedals). Confirm the wheel is Xbox licensed
  • Not included: screen and mount, shifter

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• ~130 to 140 × 60 to 70 cm of floor, permanent
  • 40 to 55 kg with seat (est)
  • Assembly 2 to 4 hours

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 1: nothing moves when you brake, so muscle memory forms
  • 8 to 9 Nm: real weight in fast corners
  • Load cell: brake by pressure, not pedal travel
  • Slower for the first sessions on a load cell, then more consistent
  • vs F1 Arcade: wheel detail equal or better, still no motion

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: biggest consistency jump per dollar
  • +: always ready to drive
  • +: base, wheel, pedals carry to Tier 3
  • −: tube frames have limited adjustment
  • −: some wheel deck flex above ~10 Nm
  • −: proprietary hole patterns and accessories
  • −: permanent floor space
  • −: cockpit is replaced at Tier 3

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Load cell pedals, if still on a basic set
  • Then the rig itself (aluminum profile)
  • Seat can move across with brackets

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Fanatec CSL DD 5/8 Nm, Moza R9, Thrustmaster T300 with T-LCM pedals
  • New direct drive prices fell in 2026: used must be clearly under today's new price
  • Check: Fanatec QR1 vs QR2 (old QR1 does not fit current wheels), shaft play, brake reads smoothly to 100%
  • Avoid: belt bases priced near new direct drive, sellers who cannot show it working
  • Warranty usually does not transfer (Fanatec, Thrustmaster)

docs.title: $1,800–$2,200
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC/console, display, dedicated space

  • Landed with seat, monitor mount, shipping, tax: $1,800 to $2,400

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• Committed, races weekly or in a league
  • Wants to stop upgrading
  • Skip if: under ~2 hours a week
  • Skip if: PlayStation and only Gran Turismo (Tier 2 gear on a better rig is enough)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• PC: Moza R12 V2 base $429 (12 Nm) + KS wheel $229 + CRP2 load cell pedals $369 + Sim-Lab GT1 Evo rig $390 + seat and brackets ~$250 + monitor mount ~$100 = ~$1,770, plus rig shipping ~$100 to $250 (est)
  • PC, alt: Simagic Alpha Evo 12 Nm $549 + P1000 pedals $469 + GT Neo wheel ~$270 + same rig and seat = ~$1,930. Close to what newer F1 Arcade rigs use
  • PlayStation / Xbox / PC: Fanatec ClubSport DD+ GT3 bundle $1,405 (base, wheel, 3 load cell pedals) + GT1 Evo $390 + seat ~$250 = ~$2,045
  • Logitech route: PRO wheel 11 Nm $1,000 to $1,200 + PRO pedals $380 + rig + seat = ~$2,020 to $2,220
  • Rigs in US stock: Trak Racer TR80S $499, RigMetal Plus $539, ASR 3 $550, NLR GTElite Lite $599
  • Rig prices exclude seat, brackets, slider, monitor mount
  • Not included: screen, shifter, handbrake

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• GT1 Evo frame: 135×58×66 cm
  • With seat, pedals, wheel: ~150×70 cm (est)
  • Plan ~2.0×1.0 m with a screen and room to get in
  • 45 to 65 kg assembled (est)
  • Assembly 3 to 6 hours, plus an evening of adjusting

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• vs Tier 2: zero flex, every angle adjustable
  • Brake you can lean on, 60 to 100 kg
  • 12 Nm: no clipping in normal use
  • vs F1 Arcade: wheel and pedals are better than the venue's
  • Missing vs F1 Arcade: body motion, giant screens

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: rig and pedals are a 10-year purchase
  • +: everything bolts on later: shifter, shakers, motion
  • +: nothing is thrown away at Tier 4
  • −: industrial look
  • −: heavy, long assembly
  • −: many small extras: brackets, T-nuts, slider, bolts
  • −: popular rigs often back-ordered

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Display: triples or VR (Tier 4)
  • Not more torque

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Aluminum profile rigs: best used buy in the hobby. Barely wear, costly to ship, so local pickup is cheap
  • Used Moza R12/R16, Simagic Alpha, Fanatec ClubSport DD, Heusinkveld Sprint pedals
  • Check: 40-series profile (30-series is flimsy), all brackets and T-nuts, pedal controller box included
  • Avoid: wood or PVC rigs priced like aluminum, pedals missing elastomers

docs.title: $3,500–$5,500
docs.text:
Assumes: existing PC with a strong GPU. Displays included

  • GPU for triple 1440p or VR: often another $700 to $1,500

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• PC driver who wants peripheral vision and immersion
  • Rally and drift fans who need a shifter and handbrake
  • Skip if: console only (one screen, no PC VR; a big TV on a Tier 3 rig is the ceiling)
  • Skip if: mostly F1 25, Forza or EA WRC (they only stretch across triples)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• Triples: Tier 3 PC build on a Sim-Lab P1X Pro rig $770 + clutch $99 + Moza HGP shifter $149 + freestanding triple stand ~$275 + 3× 27" 1440p ~$630 to $700 + bass shaker and amp ~$300 (est) = ~$3,500
  • VR: same without stand and monitors + Meta Quest 3 $600 = ~$3,200
  • Top of band: 3× 32" 1440p ~$300 each, 18 to 21 Nm base (Moza R21 Ultra $699), handbrake $99
  • Console ceiling: Fanatec ClubSport DD+ bundle $1,405 + P1X Pro + seat + Fanatec shifter ~$300 and handbrake ~$230

docs.title: Triples vs VR
docs.text:
• Triples: 140 to 170° view, see cars alongside, nothing on your face
  • Triples need: 3 identical monitors, flat or gentle curve (1500R+), a real stand, not desk arms
  • Proper triple support: iRacing, Assetto Corsa, ACC, AC EVO, Le Mans Ultimate, Automobilista 2, rFactor 2, RaceRoom
  • Stretch only: F1 25, EA WRC, Forza Motorsport
  • VR: true depth and scale, no floor space
  • VR costs: heat, face pressure, nausea for some, can't see buttons, heavy GPU load
  • Try VR before buying. Quest 3S $350 is the cheap test

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• 27" triples: ~180 cm wide × 160 cm deep (est)
  • 32" triples: ~210 cm wide (est)
  • VR: same as Tier 3, ~150×70 cm
  • 80 to 110 kg with stand and monitors (est)
  • A full day including monitor alignment and software

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• Look into the apex, see the car next to you
  • Shakers: engine, kerbs, gear shifts through the seat
  • vs F1 Arcade: better view than the venue
  • vs F1 Arcade: the buzz, not the heave and pitch

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: biggest immersion jump after the load cell
  • +: VR is the cheapest way to 1:1 scale
  • +: everything carries to Tier 5
  • −: GPU cost not in the total
  • −: triples eat a room
  • −: VR is hot and isolating
  • −: more software to maintain (SimHub, triple configs)
  • −: shakers travel through floors to neighbors

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Stronger base or an active brake pedal
  • Then motion

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Used monitors and triple stands: plentiful, low risk
  • Same model and revision matters more than price
  • Used Quest 3: ~$350 to $450 fair (est)
  • Check: dead pixels side by side, VR lens scratches, headset factory reset
  • Avoid: mixed monitor models, tight 1000R curves, sun-burned VR lenses

docs.title: $10,000–$18,000
docs.text:
Assumes: existing high-end PC, dedicated room. Displays included

  • "Motion lite" now exists at $7,000 to $9,000

docs.title: Target user
docs.text:
• This is the main hobby
  • Real-world drivers training
  • Chasing the F1 Arcade feel at home
  • Skip if: not yet consistent on Tier 3 or 4 (motion adds immersion, not pace)
  • Skip if: someone lives below you (actuators thump)

docs.title: Parts
docs.text:
• Full: Simucube 3 Pro base $1,599 (25 Nm) + wheel ~$1,000 (est) + Simucube ActivePedal Pro brake from $1,849 + throttle ~$400 (est) + D-BOX G5 4-actuator kit $6,200 to $8,250 + Sim-Lab P1X Ultimate rig $877 + seat ~$400 + 3× 32" ~$900 + stand ~$300 = ~$13,500 to $15,600
  • Motion lite: Moza R25 Ultra $899 + CS Pro wheel $329 + mBooster active pedal set $949 + Moza HMA150 4-actuator kit $2,999 + P1X Pro $770 + seat + 3× 27" + stand = ~$7,100
  • Seat mover: Tier 4 build + Next Level Racing Motion Plus $2,799 = ~$6,500 to $7,500
  • PC only: motion reads PC telemetry
  • Not included: PC, pallet freight, software licenses

docs.title: F1 Arcade comparison
docs.text:
• F1 Arcade: Vesaro rigs, D-BOX G5 actuators, custom rFactor 2
  • Newer venues: Simagic Alpha Evo base, P1000 pedals, GT Neo wheel (per Simagic)
  • So the venue is Tier 5 motion with roughly Tier 3 controls
  • The D-BOX kit alone costs more than a whole Tier 4 rig
  • This tier: same motion family, stronger wheel, better pedals

docs.title: Footprint
docs.text:
• ~210×180 cm with triples, plus clearance to move (est)
  • 150 to 200 kg without driver (est)
  • One to two days to build, weeks to tune

docs.title: What it feels like
docs.text:
• Chassis heaves, pitches, rolls
  • Kerbs and gear shifts hit the whole body
  • Active brake: ABS pulse, pad feel, different per car
  • Not faster. More real

docs.title: Pros / cons
docs.text:
• +: closest thing to the venue or a pro simulator
  • +: D-BOX and Simucube hold resale value
  • −: cost
  • −: noise and floor vibration
  • −: tuning time
  • −: little lap time gain
  • −: service means shipping heavy parts

docs.title: Next upgrade
docs.text:
• Nothing hardware
  • Coaching and seat time

docs.title: Used-market alternative
docs.text:
• Simucube 2 Sport / Pro (new $999 / $1,299), D-BOX Gen 3 to 5, Heusinkveld Ultimate+ pedals
  • Check: actuator knocking, controller box and cables present, motion software license transfers, E-stop works
  • Avoid: undocumented DIY motion, kits missing controller or brackets, sellers who won't demo under load

docs.title: Sound
docs.text:
• What: engine and tire noise
  • Why: shift timing by ear, cheap immersion
  • When: whenever. headphones are fine

docs.title: What sound tells you
docs.text:
• Tire scrub: grip is going, before the wheel says so
  • Engine note: when to shift, wheelspin
  • Other cars: who is beside you
  • Kerbs, bottoming, gravel

docs.title: Hearing it
docs.text:
Option Price Good Bad What you own $0 Free TV speakers hide detail Closed gaming headset Under $100 Blocks fan and wheel noise, has a mic Hot, narrower sound Open-back headphones (Sennheiser HD 560S) ~$200 Best positioning, cooler ears Leaks sound, lets room noise in Wireless headset, 2.4 GHz dongle $100 to $350 No cable Not Bluetooth: lag Desk or rig speakers Varies Nothing on your head, others can hear Less precise, disturbs housemates Surround speakers $300+ Real rear sound Cost, wiring. Skip
  • Mix: turn tires and other cars up, engine and wind down

docs.title: Feeling it: bass shakers
docs.text:
• A speaker-like puck bolted to the seat or rig. Plays engine, kerbs, gear shifts, wheel slip as vibration
  • Driven by SimHub on PC through a small amp
Level Kit Price Notes Starter Dayton puck on the seat ~$20 Weak. Seat or pedal plate only Default DIY Dayton BST-1 + small amp (Nobsound, Fosi) + SimHub ~$100 to $150 Best value Plug and play ButtKicker Gamer Plus / Pro $280 / $350 Amp and clamp included Four corners 4 shakers + amp $415 to $1,300 Diminishing returns
  • Best immersion per dollar. Makes you no faster
  • Works on an office chair or foldable too
  • Vibration travels through floors. Downstairs neighbors are the limit
  • Mount on the seat, not the frame, to keep it quieter

docs.title: Spotter
docs.text:
• Crew Chief (free, PC): voice calls "car left", "clear", gaps, fuel
  • On one screen you cannot see beside you. A spotter is the cheapest safety upgrade

docs.title: Ignore
docs.text:
• 7.1 "gaming surround" modes
  • Expensive sound cards
  • Bluetooth for racing

docs.title: By tier

docs.title: Sensor types
docs.text: Type Reads Notes Potentiometer Pedal position, by a rubbing contact Wears, gets jumpy Hall Pedal position, by a magnet Same feel, lasts Load cell Force on the pedal The upgrade that matters Hydraulic Usually still a load cell, with a fluid damper On cheap sets "hydraulic" means a small damper Active A motor creates the resistance Not the same as vibration add-ons

docs.title: Why a load cell
docs.text:
• Real brakes respond to pressure
  • Your leg repeats a force far better than a foot position
  • Gain: the same braking every lap. Consistency first, speed after
  • Biggest for: braking at the limit without ABS, easing off while turning in
  • Slower for the first week or two. Normal

docs.title: What matters
docs.text:
• Load cell brake
  • A mount that does not move. Chair, pedals and seat tied together
  • Adjustable stiffness (rubber stacks or springs)
  • Pedal spacing and angle that fit your feet
  • Console: must be the same brand as the wheelbase

docs.title: Ignore
docs.text:
• 200 kg vs 100 kg sensors. Nobody brakes above 60 to 80 kg
  • A clutch "just in case". Cheap to add later
  • Vibration motors sold as "active"
  • Setting it as stiff as it goes
  • Inverted (hanging) pedals, unless you want road car feel and have the rig

docs.title: Two pedals or three
docs.text:
• Two is enough: F1, GT3, prototypes, most online racing
  • Clutch needed: H-pattern shifter, drifting, trucks, some standing starts
  • Add-on clutch: $45 to $100 on most sets

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:

  • Above ~30 to 40 kg of brake force: pedals and seat on the same frame

docs.text:

docs.title: The two free wins
docs.text:
• Correct field of view (FOV)
  • Force feedback that does not clip

docs.title: Seating
docs.text:
• Wheel distance: shoulders on the seat, arm straight, wrist rests on top of the rim
  • Elbows bent ~90 to 120° at 9 and 3
  • Wheel height: top of rim around shoulder height
  • Pedals: knee still bent at full brake
  • Office chair: lock or cup the casters before anything else
  • GT position (upright, pedals low): start here. Works for everything
  • Formula position (reclined, feet high): only if you drive formula cars only

docs.title: Screen and FOV
docs.text:
• FOV = how much of the world is squeezed onto your screen
  • Game defaults are far too wide: everything looks slow and far, braking points are wrong
  • Correct FOV depends on two things: screen width and eye distance
  • Steps
    • Move the screen as close as possible, right behind the wheelbase
    • Screen center at or just below eye level
    • Measure eye-to-screen distance and screen width
    • Put the numbers in an FOV calculator, enter the result in the game
  • Correct FOV feels zoomed in at first. Give it a few sessions
Screen Eyes at 60 cm 70 cm 100 cm 27" 53° 46° 33° 32" 61° 54° 39° 34" ultrawide 67° 59° 43° 49" super-ultrawide 90° 81° 62° 55" TV at 2.5 m 27°
  • A 27" monitor at arm's length shows twice what a 55" TV across the room does
  • VR: no FOV setup. Set eye spacing (IPD) instead

docs.title: Wheel rotation
docs.text:
• Set the wheel software to its maximum (900° or more)
  • Let the game match each car automatically (iRacing, ACC, Assetto Corsa, Le Mans Ultimate do)
  • Wrong if: the on-screen wheel does not match your hands

docs.title: Force feedback
docs.text:
• Force feedback is information about front tire grip, not a strength contest
  • Clipping: the game asks for more force than the wheel has. Everything strong feels the same, detail vanishes
  • Tuning order
    • Wheel software: 100% on Logitech and belt wheels. Direct drive: a comfortable peak, often 5 to 8 Nm
    • In game: lower gain until the heaviest corner stops maxing the meter
    • Turn off fake effects (kerb, engine, road rumble), add back to taste
  • Arms ache after 20 minutes: too strong
  • Change one setting at a time

docs.title: Brake and pedals
docs.text:
• Calibrate in the maker's software first, then in each game
  • Load cell: set 100% at a force you can repeat for a whole race, not your one-time max
  • Beginner range: 20 to 40 kg
  • Small deadzone at the bottom so a resting foot does not drag the brake
  • Pick socks or shoes and stick with one

docs.title: First weeks
docs.text:
• Slower than a controller for days to weeks. Normal
  • First car: Mazda MX-5 or any slow rear-wheel-drive car, short track
  • Consistency first, speed later
  • Sessions of 30 to 60 minutes
  • ABS and traction control are not cheating. Use what the real car has

docs.title: Comfort
docs.text:
• Motion sickness on a screen: usually wrong FOV or uneven frame rate
  • VR: start with 10 to 15 minutes, stop at the first nausea, use a fan
  • Heat: a fan aimed at you is the cheapest upgrade
  • Noise: rubber mat under the rig, headphones for sound

docs.title: Free software worth installing (PC)
docs.text:
• Crew Chief: voice spotter ("car left") and race engineer. Free
  • SimHub: dash on an old phone, drives bass shakers. Free, license from 8 EUR
  • Maker software: Moza Pit House, Fanatec app, Simagic SimPro, Logitech G HUB. Update firmware first
